The lab results show normal readings, which makes a urinary tract infection unlikely given your skin symptoms. Since the rash is on your upper extremities, have you noticed any new medications, insect bites, or recent travel in the last few weeks?

REQUEST TEST: Skin biopsy, ANA (Antinuclear Antibody), and ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate).

speaker: Doctor
text: The skin biopsy findings of intraepidermal edema and widened intercellular spaces are classic for spongiosis, and with normal ANA, ESR, and CBC, we can rule out systemic autoimmune disease. Have you noticed any seasonal changes in your symptoms, or have you been exposed to any new plants, chemicals, or soaps recently? REQUEST IMAGES: Dermoscopy of the rash.

speaker: Patient
text: 23-year-old female. The patient complains of a pruritic rash on both upper extremities that has been present for 5 months. She notes that the rash occasionally worsens but has not completely resolved at any point. She denies any recent illnesses and mentions that she has not started any new medications or come into contact with any new substances that she is aware of.

speaker: Doctor
text: The biopsy showing spongiosis and your history of a pruritic rash on the arms that worsens with certain triggers strongly suggest allergic contact dermatitis. You mentioned avoiding new substances, but did you try to identify specific fabrics like wool or synthetic blends you wear, or perhaps jewelry containing nickel?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pruritic rash on the bilateral upper extremities. I also have No fever, No joint pains, No recent illnesses.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Allergic Contact Dermatitis. The clinical picture of a pruritic, spongiotic rash on the bilateral upper extremities in a young female, combined with negative systemic workup for autoimmune or infectious causes, strongly supports an allergic etiology, likely from contact with jewelry (nickel) or textile dyes.
